title: Obfuscated Files or Information: SVG Smuggling
shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: SVG Smuggling
summary: SVG smuggling hides script inside Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) files, which are vector images written in Extensible Markup Language (XML). Because script tags are a legitimate part of the format, a crafted image can carry JavaScript that the rendering context executes, and SVG content is frequently treated as an image by mail gateways, web filters and users, so it receives less scrutiny than a script or executable. The smuggled script commonly assembles a payload in the browser from encoded fragments, downloads a file, redirects the victim to a hostile site, or draws interactive content such as a fake login form or download button that collects credentials. The same technique is used on its own or nested inside a Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) page, a Portable Document Format (PDF) file or another document, which further obscures where the code originated. Defenders should treat an SVG file as executable content attached to a document: inspect it as text, look for script elements and event handler attributes, follow the network calls the render makes, and check the process tree and downloaded files afterwards. The gap that makes the technique work is a classification mistake, not a broken control, so the corrective step is to align how filters treat the format with what it can actually do.

beginner.definition: SVG files are picture files that describe a drawing with text instead of fixed dots. The full name is Scalable Vector Graphics. Because they are built from text, they can carry a small script, which is a piece of code. This is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information. The script hides inside something you think of as an image. When a browser shows the picture, the script can run.
beginner.whyItMatters: People trust pictures more than programs, so they open SVG files without worry. Many filters also treat SVG as an image and inspect it less strictly. A script inside the file can then download more harmful code or show a fake login page. The code runs as the user, so it inherits that user's access. Filtering by file type alone will not protect you here.
howItWorks: The attacker builds an SVG file, or edits a real one, so it still shows a normal picture.
They add a script tag with JavaScript, which browsers are allowed to run in SVG content.
Inside the script they store encoded pieces that can rebuild another program later.
They may instead add code that downloads a file or sends the user to another site.
The SVG reaches the victim by email, chat or a web page and looks like an ordinary image.
When it renders, the script runs quietly and does the work without any visible warning.
beginner.example: Imagine a museum display case holding a drawing on paper. A member of staff can lift the paper and find a small drawer underneath with a written instruction inside. Visitors only see the drawing, and the guards check the glass, not the paper. Because drawings are never expected to carry instructions, nobody lifts the sheet. The instruction is simple, but the hiding place is what makes it effective.
takeaways: Treat SVG files from outside your organisation as executable content, not as plain pictures.
Look for script elements and event handlers inside SVG files, especially in email attachments.
After an SVG renders, check what was downloaded and which processes started afterwards.

objectives: Explain how script tags inside Scalable Vector Graphics files can execute in a rendering context.
Describe why filters and users often treat SVG content as a harmless image.
Identify common smuggling goals, including payload assembly, downloads, redirects and fake forms.
Explain how this sub-technique relates to HTML smuggling and to SVG files nested in other documents.
Describe the network and endpoint artefacts that reveal an SVG smuggling attempt.
